## Overview

This course has focused on single containers running on a single host, like your
personal laptop or a remote workstation virtual machine. 
We point out three technologies you are likely to encounter that go beyond this 
in supporting multiple containers that are interconnected or run on multiple
hosts.


## Podman Compose: multiple containers

Many applications need several distinct services working together. A modern web
application, for example, may have a backend, a frontend (user interface) and a
database. Both Podman and Docker provide *Compose* functionality, which lets you define
a group of containers that may share storage and networking, in a
single YAML file.

Everything we have learnt about individual containers still applies: images are
built and published in exactly the same way. It is only their running as a
unified instance, i.e., their *composition*, that is new. A minimal
example compose YAML file could look like:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: ghcr.io/username/python-demo:0.0.1
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: docker.io/postgres:18
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  dbdata:
```
This defines a postgres database with persistent storage that our `python-demo`
app depends on, e.g., to store the results of each run.

::: {.callout-warning collapse=true}
## Compose and Podman

Unlike the running of individual containers, where Podman and Docker are largely interchangeable,
Podman Compose provides only a subset of features from Docker Compose. Podman can, however, interface directly
with Docker Compose, if needed
(see *Settings* > *Resources* > *Compose*).
:::

## Apptainer: containers on HPC

Docker and Podman are standard across much of science and industry, but
multi-user systems such as HPC clusters often use Apptainer (formerly
'Singularity') instead. It has many of the same features, only a slightly different syntax,
and must be run from the command line. It is also able to work with the MPI
(Message Passing Interface) installation on a cluster to run processes across
several machines at once. The
[Apptainer User Guide](https://apptainer.org/docs/user/main/) is a complete
reference and includes walkthroughs for getting started. 

::: {.callout-tip}
## Compatibility

Apptainer can run OCI images built by Podman (it
converts them to its own SIF format). The reverse is not
true: an Apptainer SIF file cannot be used directly by Podman or Docker. This is another
reason to publish your images in the OCI format on a public registry, as we have
done throughout this course.
:::

## Kubernetes: orchestration

In the next course of this series you can learn about Kubernetes, a container
*orchestration* platform. It manages applications typically comprising 
multiple containers running across several machines,
and is designed to be scalable, resilient and automated. It is increasingly used
by research software engineers and infrastructure engineers in digital research
infrastructure.

Kubernetes is *declarative*. Rather than issuing explicit commands as with Podman 
(e.g., build the image, start the container), you define a target state for
your application and Kubernetes determines how to achieve and then maintain that state.

One connection worth making now is that the smallest deployable unit in
Kubernetes is not a container but a *Pod*, which is a wrapper around one or more
containers that share storage and networking. And now for the big reveal: Podman
is designed for Pods! (Read: *Pod* *man*anger.)
Podman Desktop supports creating Pods for
your containers, and also generating Kubernetes YAML definition files (called
*manifests*)  to deploy to a Kubernetes cluster. You can explore this
yourself before the next course.

If the next course catches your interest, you may like to check out the
Cloud-Native SIG at [cloudnative-sig.ac.uk](https://cloudnative-sig.ac.uk/). We
are a community for modern cloud-native technologies in digital research
infrastructure, and deliver regular training workshops on Kubernetes.
